title: Covalent KRAS G12C inhibitors in previously treated non-small cell lung cancer
abstract: Sotorasib and adagrasib are covalent inhibitors that lock KRAS G12C in its inactive GDP-bound state. In previously treated KRAS G12C-mutant non-small cell lung cancer, both agents produced objective responses in a subset of patients, and both received regulatory approval. Responses were typically not durable, and acquired resistance emerged through secondary KRAS mutations and bypass pathway activation, including MET amplification.

title: Feedback EGFR reactivation limits KRAS G12C inhibitors in colorectal cancer
abstract: Colorectal cancer with KRAS G12C responds poorly to single-agent KRAS G12C inhibitors compared with lung cancer. Mechanistic studies show that inhibiting KRAS G12C triggers rapid feedback reactivation of EGFR signaling in colorectal cells, which restores MAPK pathway output. Combining a KRAS G12C inhibitor with an anti-EGFR antibody such as cetuximab or panitumumab improved response rates in early-phase trials of KRAS G12C-mutant colorectal cancer.

title: Osimertinib as first-line therapy for EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer
abstract: Osimertinib, a third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, is active against EGFR exon 19 deletions and L858R substitutions as well as the T790M resistance mutation. In first-line treatment of EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer, osimertinib improved progression-free survival compared with first-generation EGFR inhibitors and showed better central nervous system activity. Despite durable benefit in many patients, resistance eventually develops.

title: Mechanisms of acquired resistance to osimertinib in EGFR-mutant lung cancer
abstract: Resistance to osimertinib in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer is heterogeneous. On-target resistance includes the EGFR C797S mutation, which prevents covalent binding of the drug. Off-target mechanisms include MET amplification, HER2 amplification, activating mutations in KRAS and BRAF, and histologic transformation to small cell lung cancer. Comprehensive genomic profiling at progression, including circulating tumor DNA, guides selection of subsequent therapy.

title: Combined BRAF and MEK inhibition in BRAF V600-mutant melanoma
abstract: BRAF V600E and V600K mutations are present in roughly half of cutaneous melanomas and drive constitutive MAPK signaling. Combining a BRAF inhibitor such as dabrafenib or vemurafenib with a MEK inhibitor such as trametinib or cobimetinib improved response rate and survival compared with BRAF inhibitor monotherapy. The combination also reduced cutaneous toxicities caused by paradoxical MAPK activation in BRAF wild-type cells.

title: Encorafenib plus cetuximab in BRAF V600E metastatic colorectal cancer
abstract: In colorectal cancer, the BRAF V600E mutation defines an aggressive subtype with poor prognosis. Unlike in melanoma, BRAF inhibitor monotherapy is ineffective in BRAF V600E colorectal cancer because of rapid feedback activation of EGFR. The combination of encorafenib with cetuximab, with or without binimetinib, improved overall survival in previously treated BRAF V600E-mutant metastatic colorectal cancer in a phase 3 trial.

title: Synthetic lethality of PARP inhibition in BRCA-deficient cancers
abstract: Cells with BRCA1 or BRCA2 loss are deficient in homologous recombination repair and depend on PARP-mediated repair, a relationship termed synthetic lethality. PARP inhibitors such as olaparib and niraparib are approved for BRCA-mutated ovarian cancer. They are also approved for selected patients with breast, pancreatic and prostate cancer harboring germline or somatic BRCA alterations.

title: Reversion mutations and other mechanisms of PARP inhibitor resistance
abstract: Resistance to PARP inhibitors arises through restoration of homologous recombination, most notably by secondary reversion mutations in BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 that restore the open reading frame. Other mechanisms include loss of 53BP1 or the shieldin complex, drug efflux through upregulation of ABCB1, and stabilization of stalled replication forks. Reversion mutations can be detected in circulating tumor DNA from patients who progress on therapy.

title: Trastuzumab deruxtecan in HER2-low breast cancer
abstract: Trastuzumab deruxtecan is an antibody-drug conjugate that delivers a topoisomerase I inhibitor payload to HER2-expressing cells and exerts a bystander effect on neighboring tumor cells. It showed activity in HER2-low breast cancer, defined as immunohistochemistry 1+ or 2+ without ERBB2 amplification. This expanded the population that may benefit from HER2-directed therapy beyond HER2-positive disease.

title: HER2 heterogeneity in trastuzumab-treated gastric adenocarcinoma
abstract: HER2 overexpression or ERBB2 amplification occurs in a subset of gastric and gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinomas. Adding trastuzumab to chemotherapy improved survival in HER2-positive gastric cancer. HER2 expression in gastric tumors is heterogeneous and can change after trastuzumab exposure, which complicates biomarker testing at progression.

title: Limitations of PD-L1 immunohistochemistry as a predictive biomarker in lung cancer
abstract: PD-L1 expression measured by immunohistochemistry is an approved but imperfect biomarker for anti-PD-1 and anti-PD-L1 immunotherapy in non-small cell lung cancer. Patients with high PD-L1 expression are more likely to respond to pembrolizumab monotherapy, yet some PD-L1-negative tumors respond and some PD-L1-high tumors do not. Assay differences, tumor heterogeneity and dynamic expression limit the predictive value of PD-L1 alone.

title: Mismatch repair deficiency and microsatellite instability predict checkpoint inhibitor benefit
abstract: Microsatellite instability-high and mismatch repair-deficient tumors accumulate many frameshift mutations that generate neoantigens, making them sensitive to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Pembrolizumab received tumor-agnostic approval for MSI-H or dMMR solid tumors. In colorectal cancer, MLH1 promoter hypermethylation causes sporadic dMMR, whereas germline mutations in MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2 cause Lynch syndrome.

title: Tumor mutational burden as a biomarker for immune checkpoint blockade
abstract: Tumor mutational burden is a candidate biomarker for response to immune checkpoint blockade because higher burdens increase the probability of neoantigen presentation. A threshold of 10 mutations per megabase was used for a tumor-agnostic pembrolizumab approval. However, the predictive value of TMB varies by cancer type, and panel-based estimates differ from whole-exome measurements.

title: TP53 mutation spectrum and prognostic impact across cancers
abstract: TP53 is the most frequently mutated gene across human cancers. Most TP53 mutations are missense substitutions in the DNA-binding domain that abolish transcriptional activity, and some exert dominant-negative or gain-of-function effects. In acute myeloid leukemia, TP53 mutations are associated with complex karyotype, resistance to standard chemotherapy and adverse prognosis.

title: MDM2 inhibitors reactivate p53 in TP53 wild-type tumors
abstract: MDM2 negatively regulates p53 by promoting its degradation. In tumors with wild-type TP53, MDM2 amplification or overexpression suppresses p53 function, and small-molecule MDM2 inhibitors reactivate p53 signaling. Clinical development has been limited by on-target hematologic toxicity, and these drugs are not expected to work in TP53-mutant tumors.

title: Post-operative circulating tumor DNA and recurrence risk in stage II colon cancer
abstract: Circulating tumor DNA detected after surgery in stage II colon cancer identifies patients at high risk of recurrence. Tumor-informed assays track patient-specific somatic mutations in plasma and can detect molecular residual disease months before radiographic recurrence. Studies are testing whether ctDNA-guided adjuvant chemotherapy can safely spare ctDNA-negative patients from treatment.

title: Plasma genotyping to detect resistance mutations at progression
abstract: Plasma genotyping of circulating tumor DNA offers a non-invasive means of identifying resistance mutations, such as EGFR T790M, at disease progression when repeat biopsy is difficult. Sensitivity depends on tumor shedding and is lower in patients with limited metastatic burden or central nervous system-only disease. A negative plasma result should therefore be followed by tissue testing.

title: Clonal evolution and intratumoral heterogeneity under targeted therapy
abstract: Single-cell and multi-region sequencing show that tumors consist of multiple subclones with distinct mutations that evolve under therapeutic selection. Pre-existing resistant subclones present at low frequency can expand during targeted therapy, explaining why single-biopsy genotyping may miss resistance drivers. Spatial and temporal heterogeneity therefore motivate serial sampling and combination strategies.

title: Deep learning on H&E whole-slide images to predict molecular alterations
abstract: Deep learning models trained on hematoxylin and eosin stained whole-slide images can predict molecular features such as microsatellite instability, and in some cancers mutations including TP53 and EGFR, directly from histology. Performance varies across cohorts and slide scanners, so external validation at independent institutions is essential. These models are most plausibly used for pre-screening, to prioritize which patients receive confirmatory molecular testing.

title: Generalization of machine learning classifiers on tumor gene-expression data
abstract: Machine learning classifiers trained on tumor gene-expression profiles can predict cancer type and, in some settings, therapy response. Models trained on a single cohort often fail to generalize because of batch effects and differing sequencing platforms. Regularized linear models remain strong baselines for high-dimensional, low-sample genomic data, and nested cross-validation is required to avoid optimistic estimates caused by information leakage.

title: Alpelisib plus fulvestrant in PIK3CA-mutated hormone receptor-positive breast cancer
abstract: PIK3CA mutations occur in a substantial fraction of hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative breast cancers. The alpha-selective PI3K inhibitor alpelisib combined with fulvestrant improved progression-free survival in PIK3CA-mutated advanced breast cancer. Hyperglycemia and rash are common on-target toxicities that require proactive management.

title: ESR1 mutations and oral SERDs after CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy in breast cancer
abstract: CDK4/6 inhibitors such as palbociclib and ribociclib combined with endocrine therapy are standard first-line treatment for hormone receptor-positive advanced breast cancer. Acquired ESR1 ligand-binding domain mutations emerge under aromatase inhibitor therapy, drive ligand-independent estrogen receptor activity, and can be detected in circulating tumor DNA. Oral selective estrogen receptor degraders such as elacestrant show activity in ESR1-mutant disease.

title: ALK inhibitors and resistance mutations in ALK-rearranged lung cancer
abstract: ALK rearrangements, most commonly EML4-ALK fusions, define a subset of non-small cell lung cancer sensitive to ALK tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Alectinib and lorlatinib have greater central nervous system penetration than crizotinib and improved progression-free survival in the first-line setting. Resistance to second-generation inhibitors frequently involves ALK kinase domain mutations such as G1202R, which may remain sensitive to lorlatinib.

title: Targeting RET, ROS1 and NTRK fusions across tumor types
abstract: RET fusions, ROS1 fusions and NTRK fusions are uncommon oncogenic drivers that nevertheless have highly effective targeted therapies. Selpercatinib and pralsetinib inhibit RET, while entrectinib and larotrectinib inhibit NTRK and ROS1 fusion-positive tumors, with larotrectinib receiving tumor-agnostic approval for NTRK fusion-positive solid tumors. Detection of fusions is best achieved by RNA-based sequencing because DNA panels can miss intronic breakpoints.

title: IDH1 and IDH2 mutations: oncometabolite biology and targeted inhibitors
abstract: Mutations in IDH1 and IDH2 produce the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate, which inhibits alpha-ketoglutarate-dependent dioxygenases and causes a hypermethylation phenotype. Ivosidenib, an IDH1 inhibitor, is approved for IDH1-mutated acute myeloid leukemia and cholangiocarcinoma. Vorasidenib has shown activity in IDH-mutant low-grade glioma.

title: STK11 and KEAP1 co-mutations and immunotherapy outcomes in KRAS-mutant lung adenocarcinoma
abstract: Co-mutations in STK11 and KEAP1 are enriched in KRAS-mutant lung adenocarcinoma and are associated with poor outcomes on immune checkpoint inhibitors. Loss of STK11 is linked to an immunologically cold tumor microenvironment with reduced T-cell infiltration. KEAP1 loss activates NRF2 signaling, which promotes oxidative stress resistance and chemoresistance.

title: ABL1 kinase domain mutations and resistance in chronic myeloid leukemia
abstract: Chronic myeloid leukemia is driven by the BCR-ABL1 fusion oncogene produced by the Philadelphia chromosome translocation. Imatinib transformed the disease into a chronic manageable condition, and resistance is often caused by ABL1 kinase domain mutations. The T315I mutation confers resistance to imatinib, dasatinib and nilotinib but remains sensitive to ponatinib and asciminib.

title: FGFR alterations as therapeutic targets in cholangiocarcinoma and urothelial carcinoma
abstract: Activating FGFR2 fusions and rearrangements occur in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, and FGFR3 mutations and fusions are frequent in urothelial carcinoma. Pemigatinib and erdafitinib are FGFR inhibitors approved for these settings. Hyperphosphatemia is a characteristic on-target effect of FGFR inhibition.
